pamphlet_excerpts: Seeking Cool Shade: If you or someone in your group shows signs of a heat reaction, get to acool, shady place (p. 15).
Positioning the Heat Victim: Have the person lie down with the feet, head, and shoulders slightly raised, and remove excess clothing (p. 15).
Active Body Cooling Methods: Cool the victim any way you can (cover the person with cool, wet towels, or sponge the person with cool water; fan the person; place the victim in a stream) (p. 15).
Emergency Medical Escalation: If you do not see a rapid recovery, seek medical attention right away (p. 15).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Cool the Overheated Victim: Cool the victim any way you can (cover the person with cool, wet towels, or sponge the person with cool water; fan the person; place the victim in a stream) (p. 15).
Step 2 - Seek Prompt Medical Attention: If you do not see a rapid recovery, seek medical attention right away (p. 15).
Step 3 - Monitor for Sunburn Blistering: Most sunburns are first-degree burns, but prolonged exposure to the sun can cause blistering, a second-degree burn (p. 15).
Step 4 - Apply SPF 30 Protection: Sunburn is easy to prevent by applying plenty of sunscreen and clothing with a sun protection factor (SPF) rating of at least 30 (p. 15).

pamphlet_excerpts: Choosing Whole Versus Filleted: Keep in mind that not all fish should be filleted (p. 79).
Boneless Skinless Fillet Benefits: Removing the meat of some fish from the bones and skin makes it easier to cook and to eat (p. 79).
Initial Behind-the-Gill Cut: Lay the fish on its side and make a cut just behind the gills down to the backbone (p. 79).
Tracing the Backbone Line: Start at the cut made in step 1 and run the point of the knife alongside the backbone, down to where it starts to click along the tops of the ribs (p. 79).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Cut Behind the Gills: Lay the fish on its side and make a cut just behind the gills down to the backbone (p. 79).
Step 2 - Slice Along the Backbone: Start at the cut made in step 1 and run the point of the knife alongside the backbone, down to where it starts to click along the tops of the ribs (p. 79).
Step 3 - Free Meat From Ribs: Cut alongside the ribs, working back toward the tail until the entire side of the fish is free from the ribs and backbone, but leave it attached (p. 79).
Step 4 - Separate Fillet From Skin: Lay the side flat and hook a forefinger under the skin near the tail (p. 79).

choices: A. Cast sidearm in a crowded group without looking behind you, and yank a deeply embedded treble hook straight backward with rusty pliers.
B. Hold fish hooks between your lips while tying knots, and treat a hook near the eye by pushing it deeper with a pocketknife.

patrol_quiz_bank.question: How do nylon monofilament and fluorocarbon fishing lines differ in how they behave in the water?
options: A. Nylon monofilament floats, whereas fluorocarbon line sinks
B. Fluorocarbon line floats high on the surface, whereas nylon sinks rapidly
C. Both lines are coated with heavy plastic so they can be cast on a fly rod
D. Nylon has zero stretch, whereas fluorocarbon is woven from braided fibers
choices: A. Nylon monofilament floats, whereas fluorocarbon line sinks
B. Fluorocarbon line floats high on the surface, whereas nylon sinks rapidly
C. Both lines are coated with heavy plastic so they can be cast on a fly rod
D. Nylon has zero stretch, whereas fluorocarbon is woven from braided fibers
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Nylon monofilament floats, whereas fluorocarbon line sinks

choices: A. Store-bought minnows will immediately starve in natural lakes

patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Released baitfish can introduce invasive species, diseases, or parasites that harm native fish populations

patrol_quiz_bank.question: What should you do when practicing catch and release if a fish has swallowed the hook deep into its throat?
options: A. Pull firmly on the line until the hook pops free
B. Reach down through the gill slits with needle-nose pliers to twist the hook out
C. Cut the fishing line as close to the hook as possible and release the fish
D. Keep the fish out of the water for five minutes until its throat muscles relax
choices: A. Pull firmly on the line until the hook pops free
B. Reach down through the gill slits with needle-nose pliers to twist the hook out
C. Cut the fishing line as close to the hook as possible and release the fish
D. Keep the fish out of the water for five minutes until its throat muscles relax
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Cut the fishing line as close to the hook as possible and release the fish
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): If a fish you plan to release is deeply hooked, cutting the line as close to the hook as possible prevents fatal internal bleeding, and the hook will eventually rust away or work out (p. 88).
